keyVerseText: For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse: so: or, that they may be
rootMeaning: The Greek adjective ἀΐδιος (aḯdios) derives from the root ἀεί (aeí), meaning 'always' or 'ever.' This etymology conveys a sense of continuous, unceasing duration, emphasizing an unbroken, forward-moving existence. Unlike the more common English gloss 'eternal,' the root sense of ἀΐδιος highlights not only endlessness but also the quality of perpetuity that extends indefinitely into the future, sometimes with an implied forward directionality.
usageInScripture: The term ἀΐδιος appears only twice in the New Testament, with translations consistently rendering it as 'eternal' or 'in everlasting.' This limited but focused usage shows a clear emphasis on the unending nature of what is described, such as God's power and deity. The lexical distinction between ἀΐδιος and related terms like αἰώνιος suggests that ἀΐδιος specifically denotes everlasting duration, often understood as extending forward without end, which aligns with its use in contexts affirming God's perpetual existence.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ἀΐδιος as 'everlasting' rather than simply 'timeless' enriches our grasp of God's nature as continuously enduring through all ages. This word underscores the unceasing, forward-moving reality of God's power and divine presence, affirming that He is not subject to decay or limitation. For Christian faith, this reinforces the assurance that God's kingdom and authority will persist perpetually, providing believers with hope rooted in the certainty of His unending reign. It also distinguishes God's eternal nature from created things that are transient, highlighting His unique, everlasting existence.
keyVerseReflection: Romans 1:20 speaks of God's invisible attributes, including His 'eternal power and Godhead,' which are clearly perceived through creation. The use of ἀΐδιος here emphasizes the everlasting, unbroken power of God that has been evident 'from the creation of the world.' This eternal quality makes humanity without excuse, as God's enduring nature and divine attributes have always been manifest and accessible through the things made.
